name: A colleague answers your question by pasting it into a chatbot and forwarding the reply unread. Which statements describe responsible use of AI output instead? Select all correct statements.

answers.body: Check the output before passing it on, because the answer may be wrong and you are the one who answers for it.
answers.comment: L4, slide 4 (PDF page 4): The slide pairs "Check output" with not being a prompt-forwarding "meat proxy".

answers.body: Add your own understanding rather than acting as a pass-through between the asker and the model.
answers.comment: L4, slide 4 (PDF page 4): A meat proxy only forwards prompts and answers, adding no value.

answers.body: Forward the reply unchanged when it sounds confident, because a fluent answer has been verified by the model.
answers.comment: L4, slide 4 (PDF page 4): Fluency is not verification; the slide explicitly says to check the output.

answers.body: Forward the reply whenever the model answers quickly, treating speed as proof that the question was easy.
answers.comment: L4, slide 4 (PDF page 4): Response speed says nothing about correctness; output still has to be checked.

name: You use AI to write a status report and a README. Which writing habits does the lecture support? Select all correct statements.

answers.body: Do not produce a longer text than you would have written without AI.
answers.comment: L4, slide 5 (PDF page 5): This is the slide's emphasized recommendation.

answers.body: Ask for brief output, bullet points or key ideas, and request more only when you need it.
answers.comment: L4, slide 5 (PDF page 5): These are the top prompts listed on the slide.

answers.body: Prefer the longer generated version, treating extra length as a sign of thoroughness.
answers.comment: L4, slide 5 (PDF page 5): Long, repetitive text invites "AI;DR" (AI; Didn't Read) rather than trust.

answers.body: Paste the full response into the document and shorten it later, trusting readers to read it in full.
answers.comment: L4, slide 5 (PDF page 5): Readers skip long repetitive text ("TL;DR", "AI;DR"), so produce short text from the start.

name: A developer says: "The model has seen far more code than any human, so its output is expert-level." How does the lecture frame the limits of AI? Select all correct statements.

answers.body: Models learn from training data, which is dominated by average developers and average answers such as typical StackOverflow replies.
answers.comment: L4, slide 6 (PDF page 6): The slide asks how AI is trained, on what data, and mentions the average developer and StackOverflow.

answers.body: So output often reflects typical, average quality and needs checking, especially where expertise matters.
answers.comment: L4, slide 6 (PDF page 6): The framing is a caution against assuming expert-level quality.

answers.body: The model is trained on curated expert code and its output beats a senior developer's.
answers.comment: L4, slide 6 (PDF page 6): The slide points to the average developer, not to curated expert sources.

answers.body: Having learned from many answers, the model's average answer on routine coding tasks is correct.
answers.comment: L4, slide 6 (PDF page 6): The slide gives no basis for this; the average also contains mistakes.

name: Two people ask AI to configure a home network: one knows 10-20% of the topic, the other 0%. Which statements fit the lecture? Select all correct statements.

answers.body: The person with some knowledge can judge the answers and use common sense, because they know enough to spot a wrong one.
answers.comment: L4, slide 7 (PDF page 7): The slide contrasts 10-20% knowledge with 0% and stresses common sense.

answers.body: The person with 0% knowledge benefits most, because they have the most to learn from AI.
answers.comment: L4, slide 7 (PDF page 7): With no knowledge you cannot judge the answers or use common sense, so AI can lead you astray; knowledge still matters.

answers.body: Both get equally good results; AI removes the need to acquire knowledge of the topic.
answers.comment: L4, slide 7 (PDF page 7): The slide warns that AI can lead you astray, so knowledge still matters.

answers.body: The person with no knowledge should accept the first explanation; follow-up questions slow learning down.
answers.comment: L4, slide 7 (PDF page 7): The slide recommends asking why and learning from AI mistakes.

name: AI generated a background job processor in minutes. The happy path works and the unit tests pass, but they wait with <TT>Task.Delay(200)</TT>. Which concerns should a reviewer raise? Select all correct statements.

answers.body: Locking, cancellation support and graceful shutdown may be missing, because generated code often covers only the happy path.
answers.comment: L4, slide 8 (PDF page 8): These three omissions are listed for the AI-generated A2A component.

answers.body: Tests that wait a fixed time are timing-dependent and can be unreliable, so they do not prove the concurrency is correct.
answers.comment: L4, slide 8 (PDF page 8): The slide lists Task.Delay(200) in unit tests as a weakness.

answers.body: Passing tests prove that shutdown and concurrency are handled, since the tests would otherwise fail.
answers.comment: L4, slide 8 (PDF page 8): A passing happy path says nothing about the ignored cases.

answers.body: A fixed delay makes the tests deterministic, because the job always finishes within 200 ms.
answers.comment: L4, slide 8 (PDF page 8): A fixed delay only guesses at timing; it can pass or fail depending on load.

name: A maintenance repository gets an AI-generated large code change for a low-value side feature. A different team uses AI on a leaf repository for experiments. Which statements apply? Select all correct statements.

answers.body: The large change in the maintenance repository is risky because the value is low compared with the risk of the change.
answers.comment: L4, slide 8 (PDF page 8): The slide lists "Maintenance repo, risk was too high, side feature, large code change, low value".

answers.body: Leaf or low-risk repositories are a safer place to let AI work, since mistakes there have limited impact (interpretation).
answers.comment: L4, slide 8 (PDF page 8): "Leaf repos" are listed as the starting place; the safety reasoning is an interpretation.

answers.body: Each backlog item is worth implementing with AI, because generating code is cheap compared with writing it.
answers.comment: L4, slide 8 (PDF page 8): Cheap generation does not remove review and maintenance cost.

answers.body: A large AI change is acceptable in a maintenance repository if the happy path demo works.
answers.comment: L4, slide 8 (PDF page 8): Working demos do not offset the risk of a large, low-value change.

name: Pull requests made with AI flow into a large open-source repository. Which practices does the lecture combine with that? Select all correct statements.

answers.body: Humans review the changes that get merged.
answers.comment: L4, slide 12 (PDF page 12): "Humans review everything".

answers.body: Each fix comes with a test that proves the fix matters (fails without it).
answers.comment: L4, slide 12 (PDF page 12): "Make the test prove the fix matters".

answers.body: Overly specific tests, issues that cannot be reproduced and outdated SDKs are typical reasons PRs turn out not useful.
answers.comment: L4, slide 12 (PDF page 12), L4, slide 14 (PDF page 14): About 20% fail because tests are too specific; the not-useful list names these causes.

answers.body: Many merged AI PRs show that tests are no longer needed, with the community reporting problems instead.
answers.comment: L4, slide 12 (PDF page 12), L4, slide 13 (PDF page 13): The lecture keeps useful tests and review alongside AI contributions.

answers.body: Tests should be as specific to the changed code as possible to minimise failures.
answers.comment: L4, slide 12 (PDF page 12): Over-specific tests are named as a cause of failing PRs.

source: L4, slide 12 (PDF page 12), L4, slide 14 (PDF page 14)

name: One maintainer produces many pull requests by directing AI agents on the largest features and reviewing only lightly. What does this say about the human role? Select all correct statements.

answers.body: The human acts as a manager of agents: sets direction and coordinates the work.
answers.comment: L4, slide 16 (PDF page 16): "Manager of agents", AI plans, the human coordinates.

answers.body: Different tasks warrant different levels of trust, as when managing people, and management experience helps.
answers.comment: L4, slide 16 (PDF page 16): "Like managing people – different levels of trust"; experienced manager.

answers.body: No experience is needed, because agents do not change their mind or need direction.
answers.comment: L4, slide 16 (PDF page 16): The slide stresses experience in managing; agents do not complain but still need coordination.

answers.body: Routine bot PRs and AI-assisted PRs are the same category, both being plain automation.
answers.comment: L4, slide 15 (PDF page 15): Routine non-AI bots are counted separately from non-routine AI-assisted PRs.

source: L4, slide 15 (PDF page 15), L4, slide 16 (PDF page 16)

name: A product team ships changes every few days using AI agents and auto-merge for tests, infrastructure and some code, accepting occasional breakage. Which statements apply? Select all correct statements.

answers.body: Targeted supervision with auto-merge in selected areas lets the team move forward rapidly.
answers.comment: L4, slide 19 (PDF page 19): "Targeted super-vision", auto-merge for tests, infra and some code, releases every few days.

answers.body: A service such as Azure cannot be run this way, because breakage and missing rollback are unacceptable there.
answers.comment: L4, slide 19 (PDF page 19): "You can't do Azure this way" because of breakage and missing first-class rollback.

answers.body: Auto-merge removes the need for rollback, because merged changes are already verified.
answers.comment: L4, slide 19 (PDF page 19): The slide mentions missing first-class rollback as a known problem.

answers.body: The same supervision level suits a payment service and a prototype alike, with AI review catching the same errors in both.
answers.comment: L4, slide 19 (PDF page 19): The Azure contrast shows that the supervision level depends on risk.

name: You want an efficient workflow for using AI on code. Which advice does the lecture give? Select all correct statements.

answers.body: Use a tool that sees your code rather than copy-pasting snippets into a web chat.
answers.comment: L4, slide 10 (PDF page 10): "Don't copy-paste into web ChatGPT".

answers.body: You need not read every line, but you must be able to deep dive: ask AI what the code does, where, how and why.
answers.comment: L4, slide 10 (PDF page 10): "Don't check every LOC; be able to deep dive; ask what, where, how and why".

answers.body: Specify the task in as much detail as possible in advance to prevent wrong output.
answers.comment: L4, slide 10 (PDF page 10): The slide says "Don't overspec".

answers.body: Skip hands-on practice and rely on AI explanations instead of experience.
answers.comment: L4, slide 10 (PDF page 10): The slide says you need experience, so play with it.

name: The AI makes the same kind of mistake again in your project. Which habits does the lecture suggest? Select all correct statements.

answers.body: Ask AI to review the mistake and to find where to put instructions so it is avoided in future, while keeping the setup simple (KISS).
answers.comment: L4, slide 23 (PDF page 23): The two suggested prompts plus KISS.

answers.body: Keep notes and instructions as plain Markdown files in Git, so history is kept and AI can read them.
answers.comment: L4, slide 22 (PDF page 22): MD files for everything, GitHub for history (the AI-readability reason is an interpretation).

answers.body: Fix the mistake in the chat each time it appears, because the model remembers the correction across sessions.
answers.comment: L4, slide 23 (PDF page 23): The slide asks where to put instructions so the mistake is not repeated.

answers.body: Keep notes in proprietary formats such as OneNote, which AI reads as easily as plain text.
answers.comment: L4, slide 22 (PDF page 22): The slide recommends dropping OneNote and other formats in favour of MD files.

source: L4, slide 22 (PDF page 22), L4, slide 23 (PDF page 23)

name: You use AI as a rubber duck to prepare a talk. Which statements fit the lecture? Select all correct statements.

answers.body: Think first, then let AI generate or refine ideas, e.g. a title and abstract from your own raw notes.
answers.comment: L4, slide 24 (PDF page 24): "But THINK first" with a title-and-abstract example.

answers.body: Without your own thinking AI may apply outdated or wrong domain rules, as in the accountant using old accounting rules.
answers.comment: L4, slide 24 (PDF page 24): "If you don't THINK: accountant using old accounting rules, sales rep not into action".

answers.body: Ask AI first and think once the first answer looks wrong, because the ideas come from the model.
answers.comment: L4, slide 24 (PDF page 24): The slide asks you to think before generating ideas.

answers.body: AI can decide domain rules such as accounting for you, knowing the current rules.
answers.comment: L4, slide 24 (PDF page 24): The accountant example warns against this.

answers.body: Use AI as a rubber duck: put your own raw ideas to it and let it challenge them instead of replacing your thinking.
answers.comment: L4, slide 24 (PDF page 24): Rubber duck usage with "THINK first"; the "challenge" wording is an interpretation of the rubber-duck role.

name: Your team of five wants to introduce AI coding agents into a product that has a low-risk internal tooling module and a high-risk payment module with no easy rollback. Propose a policy: where and how much AI to allow, how changes are verified, who is responsible, and how the team reacts when the AI repeatedly makes the same mistake.
answer:
Where and how much: Start with low-risk or leaf areas (internal tooling, tests, infrastructure scripts) where targeted supervision and even auto-merge for selected parts allow fast iteration. For the payment module use tight supervision, small changes and no auto-merge: breakage and missing rollback are unacceptable there (compare "you can't do Azure this way"). Avoid large, low-value AI changes in maintenance code.
Rules for merging: Humans review all merged changes, and every fix must come with a test that proves the fix matters (fails without it).
Responsibility: The author who forwards AI output answers for it and must be able to explain the code; no meat-proxy behaviour.
Repeated mistakes: Ask AI to review the mistake and to find where to put instructions so it is not repeated; keep instructions as simple Markdown in Git (KISS).
keyPoints: Scope by risk: free AI use and selective auto-merge for internal tooling, small tightly supervised changes and no auto-merge for payments
Policy rule: humans review every merged change and each fix ships with a test that proves it matters
The author who forwards AI output is accountable and must be able to explain the code
Recurring AI mistakes are handled with recorded, simple (KISS) instructions kept as Markdown in Git
source: L4, slides 4, 8, 10, 12, 14, 19, 22, 23 (combined; policy structure is the answer's interpretation)

name: A junior colleague shows an AI-generated feature: 600 changed lines, all tests green, the demo works. Describe how you review it, which questions you put to the AI and to the colleague, and which signs would make you reject or shrink the change.
answer:
Value and risk first: Is the feature worth a large change in this code base? A large change for a low-value side feature carries more risk than benefit, so shrink or reject it.
Understand the code: You need not read every line but must be able to deep dive: ask AI what the code does, where, how and why, and ask the colleague to explain it (not a pass-through of prompts).
Look beyond the happy path: check locking, cancellation support and graceful shutdown, and error handling that generated code tends to ignore.
Test quality: tests that rely on Task.Delay, are over-specific, or would also pass without the change do not prove anything; ask for a test that fails without the fix.
Reject or shrink if: the author cannot explain the code, only the happy path is covered, or the tests prove nothing.
keyPoints: Weigh value against risk of a large change; shrink or reject it
Deep dive: ask AI what, where, how and why, and ask the author to explain the code
Check locking, cancellation, graceful shutdown and the non-happy path
Tests must fail without the change; fixed delays and over-specific tests prove nothing
Reject or shrink when the author cannot explain the code or only the happy path is covered
